title: Profit, Properly
intro: Unit 2 opens the real books. Every business lives or dies by one line.

blocks.html:
The most important line in business:

PROFIT = money in − money out

Money in is called revenue. Money out is called costs. Grace & Co. now tracks both, every day.

blocks.prompt: Monday. Revenue: £84. Costs: £31. What's the profit?
Tuesday is quiet. Revenue: £26. Costs: £31. Profit?
blocks.hint: Money out is bigger than money in. The answer goes below zero — that's called a loss.

blocks.html:
−£5 is a loss. The business paid out £5 more than it took in.

One quiet day is fine. Bosses only panic about the week — and analysts never panic at all. They add up.

blocks.prompt:
Work out profit for the rest of the week:
Wed: revenue £58, costs £22.
Thu: revenue £43, costs £43.
Fri: revenue £96, costs £38.
blocks.hint: One day at a time. Thursday is a strange one — what do you call zero profit?

blocks.prompt: Boss question. Add up the whole week: Mon £53, Tue −£5, Wed £36, Thu £0, Fri £58. What did Grace & Co. make?
blocks.hint: Add them all. The Tuesday loss takes £5 away from the total.

blocks.prompt: ★ Analyst's cut. Of the £142, which single day earned the biggest share — and roughly what fraction of the week's profit was it?
blocks.hint: Friday made £58 of £142. Is that closer to a quarter, a third, or a half?

blocks.html:
📈 Market story for the dinner table: some famous companies run at a LOSS on purpose — for years. Amazon barely made a profit for two decades while it grew huge.

Board discussion: when might losing money now be a smart plan? And when is it just… losing money? (Hint from your contagion knowledge: it depends who's lending, and how patient they are.)

done.title: Meeting adjourned ✓
done.html:
Revenue, costs, profit, loss — and your first full week of company books, including a loss day handled without blinking (Unit 1's negative numbers, earning their keep).

Next: The Margin — profit as a percentage, the number that tells you whether £142 is brilliant or barely alive.
